cards.title: Audit whether you actually have an abandoned cart flow (added-to-cart vs checkout started)
cards.summary: Most stores think they run an abandoned cart flow but the trigger is actually 'checkout started', leaving the much larger added-to-cart audience untracked and unrecovered.
cards.use_when: Auditing or rebuilding your cart/checkout recovery setup, or when your existing 'abandoned cart' flow underperforms despite being live.
steps: Open your ESP (Klaviyo, Mailchimp, etc.) and find the flow labeled 'abandoned cart' or 'abandoned checkout'. Read the actual trigger, not the name.

Distinguish the two events: 'added to cart' fires when someone puts an item in the cart on a product/landing page; 'checkout started' fires only after they click checkout and reach payment. These are one funnel step apart.

Klaviyo (via the Shopify integration) names the checkout-started flow 'abandoned cart' and adds it automatically; the added-to-cart metric is NOT installed by default. So a store can have 'an abandoned cart flow' that only catches far-down-funnel people.
Check Klaviyo > Metrics to see whether 'Added to Cart' exists. If it doesn't, you have no true cart flow and are missing everyone who carted but never reached checkout.

Install the added-to-cart snippet yourself (see the install card), then run a proper added-to-cart flow alongside the checkout-started flow. The source uses the same email content for both, cloned into two flows with different triggers.
caveats: Source is strongly worded that ~90% of brands he audits have this mislabeled flow; that is a presenter observation, not an audited benchmark.
Added-to-cart requires a manual snippet in most setups, so it is more technical than the auto-installed checkout trigger.

cards.title: Why abandonment is so high and why recovery is high-leverage
cards.summary: 70-85% of carts are abandoned and 26% of abandoners later buy the same item from a competitor, so an unworked cart flow is cash and market share leaking daily.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to invest in cart/checkout recovery, or building the internal case to prioritize it over other store work.
steps: Reframe the add-to-cart: it is only half the sale. The source argues that in a market with thousands of brands per niche, getting a cart add is not a strong buying signal, so you must keep working the lead.
Lead with the cost of inaction: every day a recovery flow is not live, abandoners are slipping away, and 26% of them reportedly buy the abandoned item from a competitor instead.
Segment abandoners by the reason they left so you can address each: hard objection (they weren't convinced), distraction (kid threw a plate), or 'buy later' intent (waiting for a paycheck).

Note that abandonment is now partly a browsing behavior: 59% of shoppers abandon just from browsing and use the cart as a 'save for later' / bookmark, like an Instagram like. That audience still needs a reminder.

Recognize that more than 30% of shoppers plan to buy later but don't, because they forget, change their mind, or spend the money elsewhere. Automated reminders exist to beat the forgetting and the competitor.
caveats: Statistics in the source (70-85% abandonment, 26% competitor purchase, 59% browsing, 30% plan-to-buy-later) are cited to external sources but presented without method detail; treat as directional.
The 'burning cash' framing is the presenter's opinion about the opportunity cost of an inactive flow.

cards.title: Design the recovery flow around the customer's decision cycle, not 1-2 emails
cards.summary: A short recovery flow lets customers off the hook before they finish their real multi-day decision cycle, so extend it to a long, spread-out series with branching.
cards.use_when: Planning the length, spacing, and branching of an abandoned cart/checkout email sequence.
steps: Don't stop at one or two emails over a couple of days. The source's target is a flow of roughly 6-8 emails (plus discount/support branches) spread across about 10 days to 1-2 weeks, to match a two-week decision window.

Map why length matters: multiple reminders stop customers forgetting, keep you top of mind, give room to overcome objections, let good content out-position competitors, and give time for a considered decision.

Branch the flow instead of sending one generic series: split by product/collection left behind (for product-specific info and testimonials), and split by prior-purchase status (for whether to offer a discount).
Sequence by job: quick reminders first, then product-specific education and social proof, then a last-chance urgency email, then a buyer/non-buyer split into support vs discount emails.
Keep the added-to-cart and checkout-started flows separate triggers but duplicate the same content so you maintain one set of emails.
caveats: Length and spacing are the source's stated best practice, not a universal rule; every brand differs and the outline is a starting point, not a finished system.
Spacing/timing should be tested for your audience rather than assumed.

cards.title: Write plain, item-first recovery copy that overcomes objections
cards.summary: Recovery emails should skip fluff and let the dynamic display of the actual abandoned item carry the sale, with copy aimed only at removing uncertainty.
cards.use_when: Writing copy for any abandoned cart or checkout email.
steps: Make the item the number-one feature. Showing the exact product they left behind via dynamic product sections is described as carrying ~80% of the selling, so don't bury it under graphics or long copy.
Keep copy short and to the point; the source states too many words or graphics distract the customer from completing the order.
Focus copy on overcoming objections only: quick points on shipping, product use, customer reviews, and answers to FAQs.
Use second-person, item-specific wording ('your order ships free') rather than generic broadcast copy ('all orders ship free') so it reads as addressed to them.
Answer the questions a hesitant buyer would ask (is it healthy, how long does it last, when will it arrive) with concise facts, not a blog article.
The source's stated purpose of every recovery email is narrow: remind, give the specific info needed to decide, and remove uncertainty about the buying process.
caveats: The '80% carried by the item' figure is the presenter's estimate, not a measured benchmark.
Tone can flex (one example uses playful copy), but the source still keeps product-specific substance central.

cards.title: Conversion-optimized recovery email layout
cards.summary: Recovery email designs should be short and focused, with a clear headline, an immediately visible CTA, the abandoned item with details, and trust/reassurance elements.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing the template/layout for abandoned cart and checkout emails.
steps: Put a clear headline at the top that addresses the cart or states the value proposition (e.g., 'your order ships free').
Place a prominent CTA button very high in the email so the customer can click without scrolling after opening.
Display the abandoned item with all relevant info (name, price, image, link) via dynamic content.
Add supporting sections/icons only if they are useful: shipping info, use of product, reviews.
Stack risk-reversal and trust badges such as free returns, free return shipping, buy-now-pay-later, warranty, and 'talk with an expert'.
Keep the whole design short and sweet — the source repeatedly warns against fancy graphics and long layouts for recovery emails.
caveats: The layout principles are general recommendations; the specific example email (footwear brand) is illustrative, not a guaranteed result.
Fewer elements per email risks needing more emails to cover all objections, which the source accepts as part of the spread-out flow.

cards.title: Email 1: the 30-minute quick reminder
cards.summary: The first recovery email is a near-pure reminder that shows the abandoned item and gets the warm, distracted customer over the edge.
cards.use_when: Setting up the first message and its send delay in a cart/checkout recovery flow.
steps: Time it short: the source typically sees best results sending email 1 about 30 minutes after abandonment; test 30/45 minutes against 1 hour and 4 hours, with 30-45 minutes usually winning.
Keep the email minimal: 'take another look / we saved your items' plus a 'complete my order' CTA — do not add fancy graphics or extra words that distract.
Show the specific items left behind via the dynamic product section.
Add a short social proof line and risk reversals (e.g., ships in 1-3 days, free swatches) to nudge hesitant buyers.
Purpose is narrow: simply remind the customer what they left behind and let them finish the order.
caveats: The 30-45 minute timing is the presenter's observed best result; validate on your own list.
A 'quick reminder' converts because the customer is still warm — it won't rescue cold or high-objection visitors.

cards.title: Email 2: second reminder with expanded social proof
cards.summary: The follow-up reminder repeats the simple format but leans harder on social proof and risk reversal to catch people who needed another look or were waiting on a paycheck.
cards.use_when: Writing the second message in a recovery flow, roughly a day after the first.
steps: Reuse email 1's simple structure but add more social proof and risk-reversal than the first send.
Aim it at two groups: those who just needed another reminder, and those who were waiting (paycheck) or comparing competitors.

Include: a quick remark about the product, the dynamic product section, then expanded social proof and risk reversals (e.g., free shipping, free return shipping, buy-now-pay-later, warranty, chat with an expert).
Keep it simple and similar to email 1 rather than inventing a new format.
Let the extra reassurance carry skeptical buyers who weren't ready off a pure reminder.
caveats: Same structure as email 1 means the value depends on the strength of your actual proof and guarantees, not the reminder itself.
Timing is 'about a day later' per the source; adjust to your cycle.

cards.title: Emails 3-4: split by product for specific info, then specific testimonials
cards.summary: Branch the flow by the abandoned product to deliver product-specific information and then product-specific testimonials, which the source says convert skeptical customers better than generic proof.
cards.use_when: Building branching logic in the flow and creating product/collection-specific recovery content.
steps: Add a Klaviyo conditional split (or trigger split) based on which SKU/product/collection was left behind; you don't need one branch per product, a few main collections are enough.

Email 3 gives product-specific information and overcomes objections specific to that product — e.g., for a cereal, the nutrition facts (sugar, carbs, protein, fiber, gluten-free) and how it compares. Keep it to the necessary facts, not a long article.
Email 4 follows with testimonials specific to that same product (e.g., jacket abandonment gets jacket reviews, a 4.9/5 star rating with review count, customer quotes).
The source's stated reason: a product-specific testimonial converts higher than a generic website testimonial in abandonments, because it speaks directly to the item and the person.
Continue to include the dynamic product section in both.
Show proof of why this works via A/B tests — the source cites a product-display test that produced ~6x more conversions (1 vs 6 purchases) on a higher-ticket product despite lower opens.
caveats: ~6x conversion on a product-display test is a single cited test example, not a promised outcome.
Targeting like the disease/health claims in the cereal example may carry compliance considerations in some categories.

cards.title: Email 5: last-chance urgency email
cards.summary: Once the customer has all the info, send a sparse urgency email with a hard deadline to push an impulse order, and reopen shopping to other options.
cards.use_when: Writing the mid-to-late recovery email that precedes the discount/support branch.
steps: Assume the customer now has the info from the product-specific and testimonial emails; the job of this email is to make them act.
Go hard on urgency: a harsh deadline and 'your order is expiring' framing to trigger an impulse finish.
Keep the format light: dynamic product section, urgency copy, social proof/risk-reversal icons, and finish-order CTA.
Add a 'keep shopping' option because some people simply don't want that specific item — by this point (roughly day five / fifth email) showing alternatives can re-capture them.
The source's rationale for delaying the 'keep shopping' suggestion: stay focused on the abandoned item in early emails, then broaden at the last-chance stage.
caveats: Harsh deadlines only work if they are credible; the source stresses being strict on last-chance deadlines, so don't make deadlines you don't honor.
Source preference for delaying 'keep shopping' is an opinion about focus, not a validated rule.

cards.title: Email 6A: buyer branch — founder support email, no discount
cards.summary: For customers who have bought before, send a personal founder touch offering support and a final chance instead of a discount.
cards.use_when: Configuring the prior-purchase branch in a recovery flow and writing the no-discount variant.
steps: Split the flow on whether the customer has purchased before; send this no-discount variant to past buyers only.

Make it a plain text-style email from the founder (e.g., 'hey it's Mike, co-founder') to stand out from the rest of the sequence — the source notes this personal touch can make it one of the best-performing emails in the flow.

Order the content: personal touch about the abandoned item, then an offer of support ('reply to this email, we'll get back to you within 24 hours'), then a final chance to order with a short urgency window.
Keep it simple: founder voice, last chance, support offer.
Rationale given: past buyers are the segment you least want to discount, and an unaddressed objection could be the reason for abandonment, so offering help may recover the sale without margin loss.
caveats: The claim that this can be the best-performing email is the presenter's opinion based on client experience, not a guarantee.
A 24-hour reply promise requires you can actually meet it; slow support could backfire.

cards.title: Email 6B: discount opener for first-time buyers, then a discount last-chance
cards.summary: For non-buyers, offer a simple flash discount with urgency, then follow with a discount last-chance email; keep both extremely simple and focused on the offer and the abandoned items.
cards.use_when: Setting up the non-buyer branch of a recovery flow that uses a discount to acquire first-time customers.
steps: Send this branch only to customers who have never purchased, so the discount isn't given away to buyers who would convert without it.

Email 6B: state the flash discount plainly (e.g., $10 off $200+) with urgency, plus the dynamic product section and a finish-my-order CTA. No elaborate graphics — the source says the dynamic section carries the load.
Email 7 (discount last-chance): heavy urgency on the discount ('last chance, 25% off your cart, code expires today'). Keep it minimal and strict on the deadline.

Email 8: for discount recipients who still didn't buy, mirror the founder support email but include the discount — personal founder touch, last chance to claim with the discount for a set window, and an offer of support with a reply-to-email.

Rationale given: first-order discounts are accepted because once someone tries the product they're much more likely to come back, so the discount is an acquisition cost, not a margin giveaway to loyal buyers.
caveats: Whether to discount at all, and the size/value threshold, is the presenter's choice ('depending on how averse you are to discounts'); he typically discounts only non-buyers or non-buyers in the last 60-90 days.
Discount depth and urgency must be honored; non-credible deadlines hurt trust.

cards.title: Install the added-to-cart metric and trigger in Klaviyo
cards.summary: The added-to-cart event requires a two-step manual install (snippet on site, then verify in Klaviyo) because it is not added automatically like checkout-started.
cards.use_when: Setting up or troubleshooting a true abandoned cart flow that captures add-to-cart abandoners.
steps: Check Klaviyo > Metrics. If 'Added to Cart' is missing, you need to install it. Verify against Klaviyo's current help doc since the interface changes.
On the Shopify store, if your theme has custom liquid blocks and a section you can edit, go to the homepage/product section and paste the provided snippet in a custom liquid block, then Save.

If you don't have an editable custom liquid block, edit theme code instead: insert the snippet under the body tag, wrapped with an 'if product' condition above and 'endif' below, per the guide, then Save.
Test the snippet: append a UTM (email=whatever@youwant.com) to your store URL, visit the store, and add an item to the cart.
In Klaviyo, search the email from the UTM and open the profile's activity feed; confirm an 'Added to Cart' event appears and the metric now exists.

Set the flow trigger to 'Added to Cart' with filters: checkout started 0 times (so checkout abandoners route to the checkout flow instead), placed order 0 times, and not in this flow in the last 30 days. For the checkout-started flow, use the same filters minus the checkout exclusion.
caveats: Klaviyo's snippet and metric setup can change; verify against Klaviyo's current documentation rather than relying on a saved snippet.
Editing theme code incorrectly can break the store; the source says to contact Klaviyo support to get the correct dynamic sections if you get stuck.

cards.title: Set up dynamic abandoned-item content (careful: cart and checkout variables differ)
cards.summary: Dynamic product sections are the core of recovery emails, but the added-to-cart and checkout-started variables are different, so content built for one won't work in the other.
cards.use_when: Building the item-display block in recovery emails and troubleshooting broken/altered images or links.
steps: For added-to-cart dynamic content, use a split block: image on the left using the event image URL variable, and text on the right with item name and price variables. Point the checkout/cart link to your cart page (e.g., yoursite.com/cart) if you have one, otherwise Klaviyo's link sends them to the item they viewed.
For checkout-started, the dynamic content is built as a table block that must be set to dynamic and customized, and it exposes more data because checkout passes more information from Shopify.
Always preview with Klaviyo's preview feature to confirm the dynamic content loads before the flow goes live.
Do not copy checkout dynamic content into the cart flow (or vice versa) — the triggers feed different information, so the variables won't map correctly.
If the dynamic sections won't work, ask Klaviyo support (chat) for the correct variables for your trigger.
caveats: Exact variable names and block options can change in Klaviyo; confirm current behavior in the app or with support.
Source says ideally you have a cart page; without one, the fallback link sends people to a single item, which is a weaker recovery experience.

cards.title: Set up A/B tests inside the flow rather than on the email
cards.summary: The source prefers a conditional random-sample split within the Klaviyo flow over Klaviyo's built-in email test, because numbers are visible in the flow at a glance.
cards.use_when: Running experiments on recovery emails and wanting quick visibility into results.
steps: Add a conditional split to the flow and create a random sample so branches split the audience evenly.
Copy and paste the prior email into one branch as the variant.
Reconnect the flow so both branches rejoin the main path afterward.

Compare against Klaviyo's native 'create a test' option on the email itself; the source finds that harder to read because you must click into the email to see the data, whereas the flow method shows the numbers at a glance.
Use the flow-level view to decide winners and iterate.
caveats: The preference for flow-level splits is the presenter's workflow opinion, not an accuracy claim; both can be valid.
Random-sample sizing and statistical significance are not covered here — don't over-read small test results.

cards.title: Small A/B tests can compound into large revenue gains
cards.summary: The source argues small, iterative A/B tests on recovery emails (subject lines, format, layout) can each add meaningful revenue that compounds, so the outline is only a starting point.
cards.use_when: Planning an ongoing optimization cadence for cart/checkout flows after initial launch.
steps: Treat the provided email outline as a starting point, not a finished system; every brand needs its own optimizations.
Test small iterations, because the source says small changes can make or break the success of abandonment flows.

Prioritize tests the source ran: subject line (one cited test tripled placed-order rate and roughly doubled click rate on the same volume), long-form vs short-form email (short-form reportedly better), content alignment (center vs left, cited at ~$5K extra in a month), product display (cited at ~6x conversions), text-based layout (cited at ~40% conversion boost), and email content (cited at ~2x conversions).
Do the math on compounding: the source frames repeated 25-50% revenue boosts as compounding over time, using a Warren Buffett analogy.
Run tests continuously rather than as one-offs, and pick one variable per test to keep results readable.
caveats: All the percentage examples are the source's reported client test results, not guaranteed outcomes; do not treat them as benchmarks.
The 25-50% revenue-boost range is the presenter's characterization of small-test upside; actual lift depends on your baseline and traffic.

cards.title: Separate cart and checkout flows to avoid double-messaging
cards.summary: Because added-to-cart and checkout-started are different funnel events, you need two flows with exclusion filters so people aren't messaged twice or dropped from the wrong sequence.
cards.use_when: Configuring the triggers and filters of both recovery flows in Klaviyo.
steps: Build two flows: one triggered by 'Added to Cart', one triggered by 'Checkout Started'. Duplicate the same content into both so you maintain one set of emails.

On the added-to-cart flow, add filters: 'Checkout Started = 0 times since starting this flow' (so anyone who moves to checkout exits and enters the checkout flow instead), 'Placed Order = 0 times since starting this flow', and 'has not been in this flow in the last 30 days'.

On the checkout-started flow, use the same 'Placed Order = 0 times since starting this flow' and 'not in this flow in the last 30 days' filters, without the checkout exclusion (it's the trigger itself).
Confirm both flows fire correctly and that a person who adds to cart then proceeds to checkout doesn't receive both sequences simultaneously.
caveats: The 'last 30 days' re-entry window is the source's reset choice; adjust to your purchase frequency.
Exclusion logic depends on trigger direction; verify in Klaviyo that your filters behave as intended.

cards.title: Adapt to the 2024 more-competitive buyer who does due diligence
cards.summary: With more stores and a warier, thinner-walleted buyer who shops around, recovery messaging must overcome distrust and comparison shopping, not just remind.
cards.use_when: Setting the tone and content strategy of recovery and lifecycle messaging in a crowded niche.
steps: Assume the buyer has been burned online before (late shipping, not just non-delivery), so proactively answer logistics and quality questions: when will it arrive, will it arrive intact, what do reviews say, how long does it last.
Assume the buyer is comparing you against many other brands in the same niche and may have added competitors' items to their cart too; your objection handling and content quality decide the win.
Lead with risk reversal and specifics (shipping time, returns, warranty, reviews) rather than broad claims.
Recognize shopping is entertainment for many buyers and carting is a bookmarking behavior, so reminders — not pressure — are often what's needed.
Account for tighter budgets versus the stimulus-era spend; a discount targeted only at non-buyers can help first-time acquisition.
caveats: This 2024 framing is the presenter's market read; timing-specific claims may age.
Not every niche has thousands of brands or scam-scarred buyers — calibrate the level of proof to your category.
